o:
We must go from step 0 to step n, jumping 1–3 steps at a time. Landing on step j costs costs[j] plus the squared jump distance. This is a shortest-path problem on a line with constant jump reach, so dynamic programming over steps works: the best cost to reach step i depends only on the best costs of the previous three steps. Constraints (n up to 1e5) rule out exponential path enumeration but make an O(n·3) DP trivial.

Example 1: dp builds 0→2→5→..., and reaching step 4 optimally via 0→1→2→4 gives 2+3+8=13. Example 2 shows skipping steps can help: 0→2→4 costs 5+6=11, which the DP naturally considers because it tries all three jump lengths.
k: dp[i] = min cost to stand on step i; transitions look back at most 3 steps
The squared-distance penalty is a constant per transition, so no extra data structure is needed
Answer is dp[n]; dp[0]=0 since we start free

a.i: Process steps left to right. For each step i, try jumping from each of the previous three steps; the squared distance is known from the gap, so each transition is O(1). Only 3 predecessors matter, so total time is O(n).
s: For i from 1 to n, for d in 1..3 with i-d >= 0, relax dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i-d] + costs[i-1] + d*d)
a.sp: O(n) — one DP array (reducible to O(1) with three rolling variables)

w: The DP is the intended solution; there is no meaningfully faster asymptotic approach since reading input is already O(n). Pitfalls: forgetting that costs are 1-indexed (offset by one in 0-indexed code), and integer overflow of d*d plus accumulated costs in fixed-width languages — use 64-bit intermediates. A follow-up might ask for the actual path: store parent pointers during relaxation.
